summary: Northbridge asked for a detailed walkthrough of Redwood’s Standard Cost Model (SCM): what it is (technical cost attribution/estimation, not billing), what inputs it requires (model, region/SKU, token metering, prefill/decode split, effective batch size, KV cache hit rate, quant profile), and what outputs they can expect (total cost + breakdown + assumptions + confidence). Redwood explained the difference between “estimate” and “metered attribution,” how Console uses the breakdown for transparency, and how Optimize runs what-if scenario sweeps (batching/caching/quant profile candidates) while guarding against low-confidence recommendations. Discussion included telemetry gaps, missing-signal behavior, cardinality limits, and audit logging for customer-sensitive cost views.

Inputs required for deterministic results across regions/hardware
Breakdown taxonomy: compute vs memory/overhead vs cache/batch efficiency effects

Optimize what-if sweeps and recommendation guardrails
Security/audit logging and access controls for cost breakdown reads
transcript:
Fireflies.ai Transcript (auto-generated)

Title: Northbridge AI x Redwood — Standard Cost Model (SCM) technical deep dive
Date: 2025-02-06
Start time: 10:00 AM PT
Duration: 57 min

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Aditya Rao, Priya Natarajan, Logan Wright, Hassan Mirza, Jordan Lee
Northbridge AI: Samir Patel, Lena Wu, Grace Kim, Miguel Torres

---

[00:00] Aditya Rao: Cool. Alright, thanks everyone for making time. This is Aditya. I’m on the Optimize side but we pulled in Priya and Logan since this gets pretty telemetry-heavy. The goal today is a deep dive on the Standard Cost Model, SCM, and how it shows up in Console and Optimize.

[00:18] Samir Patel: Yep, thanks. We’ve got a bunch of internal questions from FinOps. Mostly like, “how real is the cost breakdown,” and what’s actually measured versus guessed.

[00:27] Grace Kim: And also, just to be explicit, we’re not asking you to change billing right now. We need internal unit economics and showback per route.

[00:35] Aditya Rao: Perfect. That matches our scope. SCM is not the invoice. It’s a technical cost estimate / attribution model. Deterministic given inputs, and explainable. Billing/pricing is a separate layer.

[00:47] Priya Natarajan: Hey all, Priya here. I own the platform service that will answer these SCM requests. Happy to go into the API behaviors too—timeouts, versioning, that kind of thing.

[00:58] Logan Wright: Logan, telemetry. If we start talking about “what signals do you need,” I’m the person to blame.

[01:04] Miguel Torres: Miguel from SRE. I’m mostly here to understand blast radius. If this is a hard dependency and it goes down, what happens.

[01:12] Aditya Rao: Great. So, agenda: (1) what SCM is, (2) the breakdown components, (3) what inputs and telemetry it needs, (4) “estimate” vs “explain” vs “metered attribution,” and (5) Optimize what-if flows. Sound good?

[01:25] Samir Patel: Yep.

[01:27] Lena Wu: Works.

---

[01:30] Aditya Rao: Okay. SCM is basically a canonical schema and a service that returns “total_cost” and “breakdown” for an inference workload. The reason we’re doing this is: right now every team had their own spreadsheet logic, and Console numbers didn’t match Optimize recommendations, and neither matched runtime reality. SCM makes those consistent.

[01:52] Grace Kim: When you say “cost,” is it dollars? or like GPU seconds?

[01:57] Aditya Rao: Both, but with a hierarchy. The stable internal unit is normalized compute-time and resource attribution, and then we can map to a currency with a “rate table.” In outputs we generally include: (a) normalized resource units and (b) an estimated currency amount. But again, not invoice-grade.

[02:16] Jordan Lee: Jordan here—one of the things we’re strict about is “same inputs => same outputs.” So even if the underlying infra changes, the SCM version locks the semantics. If we change the mapping, it becomes a new version.

[02:32] Samir Patel: Right, that’s the determinism thing. We’ve been burned by “cost model changed overnight.”

[02:37] Aditya Rao: Exactly. We also carry “assumptions” and a “confidence” field, so if we had to infer something because telemetry is missing, we tell you explicitly.

[02:49] Lena Wu: Is confidence like a percentage?

[02:51] Aditya Rao: It’s a numeric score plus a bucket. It’s not a statistical guarantee, more like “how many required signals were present” and “how stale were reference tables,” plus a few heuristics.

[03:04] Logan Wright: And if it’s low confidence, Optimize will refuse to produce a recommendation delta. That’s a guardrail we added because otherwise you get misleading “save 37%” that’s actually just “we guessed wrong.”

---

[03:18] Priya Natarajan: Maybe we start with the taxonomy, since that’s usually where debates start. SCM breakdown is aligned to serving realities. Core components we expose:
- compute (prefill + decode)
- memory / KV-cache overhead (not always separate depending on deployment)
- batch efficiency adjustment
- cache savings (prefix/KV cache hits)
- “platform overhead” (request routing, serialization) which is small but we track

[03:45] Miguel Torres: That’s already more detailed than most vendors.

[03:49] Grace Kim: I like the “cache savings” as a line item. Because right now engineering claims “we enabled caching, it’s cheaper” and finance sees no change.

[03:58] Aditya Rao: Yep, that’s a common story. One nuance: SCM can report “cache_savings_estimated” but it depends on whether we have actual hit rate telemetry. If we don’t, we might default to “assume cold” and you’ll see no savings with a note.

[04:13] Lena Wu: When you say cache, you mean… the prompt cache?

[04:15] Logan Wright: Two things. Prefix cache (sometimes called prompt cache) and KV cache reuse. Internally we mostly track KV cache hit rate at the scheduler/runtime layer. People say “prompt cache” but it’s often KV reuse.

[04:28] Lena Wu: Got it.

[04:31] Samir Patel: What about like, GPU type differences? We run A100 in one region and H100 in another.

[04:37] Priya Natarajan: That’s a first-class dimension. Inputs include “region” and “gpu_sku.” In Dedicated and Hosted we can resolve that automatically. In Private you can either provide it or we can learn it if you integrate our node inventory exporter.

[04:54] Samir Patel: So SCM needs to know the hardware.

[04:56] Priya Natarajan: Yes, because the same token counts have different cost curves by SKU and quant profile.

---

[05:10] Aditya Rao: Let’s talk about inputs. The canonical inputs are basically: model identifier + version, deployment mode, region, GPU SKU, quantization profile, and request-level usage: input_tokens, output_tokens.

[05:26] Jordan Lee: And then “signals” that improve attribution: prefill_time_ms, decode_time_ms, batch_size_effective, kv_cache_hit_rate, and admission control outcomes.

[05:37] Miguel Torres: Admission control?

[05:39] Jordan Lee: Like whether the request was queued, merged into a batch, or rerouted. If batch_size_effective is computed before admission control you can overstate efficiency. We fixed a bug there recently actually.

[05:53] Logan Wright: Yeah, we had “batch size effective” being captured too early, and SCM was over-crediting batching. It’s fixed in the new instrumentation.

[06:03] Lena Wu: Is the batch size effective per token?

[06:06] Logan Wright: It’s typically per decode window, aggregated. We avoid per-token tagging because cardinality explodes. But we can provide an effective average for the request.

[06:19] Grace Kim: Sorry, I’m not super technical—why do you care about batch size?

[06:23] Aditya Rao: Batching amortizes GPU overhead across multiple requests. So your “compute cost per token” goes down as effective batch goes up, up to a point. SCM uses that to attribute savings.

[06:38] Grace Kim: Makes sense.

---

[06:42] Samir Patel: Can you define “estimate” vs “attribution”? Like, we want to run what-if, but also want to audit a real run.

[06:50] Aditya Rao: Yep. Two modes:
1) Estimate: given hypothetical inputs (tokens, batch policy, cache hit rate assumption, quant profile), SCM returns a predicted cost. This is what Optimize uses heavily.
2) Metered attribution / explain: given a real request_id or trace context, SCM uses runtime telemetry (prefill/decode counters, cache hits, effective batch) to attribute actual resource consumption as best as possible.

[07:16] Priya Natarajan: In API terms we have an /estimate endpoint and an /explain endpoint. Explain tends to include “contributing_factors” for tooltips and debugging.

[07:26] Miguel Torres: Does explain require you to store traces?

[07:29] Logan Wright: Not full traces. We rely on structured metrics + a short-lived event stream. For longer retention, Console aggregates. But request-level explain needs a key to fetch the per-request signals. There are controls for retention so we’re not keeping raw payloads.

[07:48] Samir Patel: So no prompts stored?

[07:50] Priya Natarajan: Correct, SCM does not need prompt text. It needs token counts and timing counters, plus IDs like model/quant profile.

[08:00] Grace Kim: That’s important for our compliance folks.

---

[08:06] Hassan Mirza: Hassan here, I work on the recommendation engine in Optimize. Just to connect it: Optimize creates a “scenario set” like: baseline config vs candidate configs. Candidates may change batching policy (on/off, max batch tokens), caching policy (warm vs cold), or quant profile (fp16 vs int8-ish), then calls SCM estimate for each scenario and compares deltas.

[08:30] Lena Wu: Wait you can model “warm cache” even before we run it?

[08:34] Hassan Mirza: We can, but that’s where assumptions come in. If you tell us “expected cache hit rate is 0.35,” we can estimate savings. If you don’t, we either (a) default to cold or (b) use historical hit rate by route if available. Confidence changes accordingly.

[08:53] Samir Patel: That’s the part we want. We can provide expected hit rates for some endpoints.

[09:00] Hassan Mirza: Great. For what-if, we also cap the scenario sweep size. Like we won’t let someone send 10,000 scenarios in one request. We usually do 20–200.

[09:13] Miguel Torres: Rate limiting and that?

[09:15] Priya Natarajan: Exactly. SCM service is a shared dependency so we have quotas. For internal Optimize we batch requests and use caching.

---

[09:28] Grace Kim: Can you show an example output? Even if it’s made up. Like what fields we’d see.

[09:34] Aditya Rao: I’ll describe a typical response. You’d get:
- total_cost: {currency: USD, amount: 0.00082}
- breakdown: compute_cost, cache_savings, batch_savings, overhead_cost
- units: maybe gpu_ms or “normalized_gpu_ms”
- assumptions: list like “kv_cache_hit_rate assumed 0.0 due to missing telemetry”
- confidence: like 0.86 and “high”

[10:03] Jordan Lee: And for explain, you’ll also get factors like “effective_batch_size: 6.3,” “prefill_tokens: 1200,” “decode_tokens: 250,” “quant_profile_id: qpf-int8-v3,” “gpu_sku: h100-80gb.”

[10:20] Lena Wu: Do you separate prefill and decode in the cost?

[10:24] Aditya Rao: Yes. Prefill is often the expensive chunk for long prompts; decode is the per-token stream. SCM tracks them separately because optimizations differ.

[10:35] Samir Patel: That’s good. Our workloads are RAG heavy, so prefill dominates.

---

[10:44] Logan Wright: On telemetry: to do the split correctly, the runtime must emit prefill and decode counters. If you’re on Hosted or Dedicated with Redwood runtime, we already do. In Private, you need to enable the instrumentation flags. There’s a small overhead budget, we target under 1% runtime overhead.

[11:02] Miguel Torres: And if we don’t enable it?

[11:04] Logan Wright: Then SCM falls back to token-based heuristics: it estimates prefill vs decode time based on tokens and model family. That reduces confidence and the breakdown will be less accurate.

[11:18] Samir Patel: Is that the “missing signal” behavior?

[11:20] Logan Wright: Exactly. We don’t silently hallucinate. We say “assumed prefill/decode split using model default curve.”

[11:28] Grace Kim: And that shows in Console?

[11:31] Priya Natarajan: It can. Console can choose to show a badge “estimated” and an “assumptions” tooltip. It depends on feature flags.

---

[11:44] Lena Wu: How do you deal with different model families? Like llama vs mistral vs… (I don’t know what all you host).

[11:51] Aditya Rao: We keep model metadata in a catalog. SCM uses that to know architecture class, typical kernel paths, and expected compute per token under different quant profiles.

[12:04] Jordan Lee: Important point: SCM doesn’t try to simulate kernels in real time. It uses measured reference tables keyed by (model_family, context_length_bucket, gpu_sku, quant_profile). That’s how we stay fast and deterministic.

[12:20] Samir Patel: Does that mean the cost model is only as good as those tables?

[12:23] Aditya Rao: Yes, but we continuously validate. We run canaries that compare SCM estimates vs metered attribution on a fixed prompt set. If drift exceeds thresholds, we alert.

[12:36] Miguel Torres: So you have mismatch detection.

[12:38] Priya Natarajan: Yep. It’s part of our SLO monitoring.

---

[12:45] Grace Kim: SLOs—what are they? Like if this is powering Console pages and it’s slow, our team will yell.

[12:52] Priya Natarajan: For Hosted/Dedicated Console views we aim p95 under ~150ms for estimate calls, and explain can be higher, like 300–500ms depending on lookups. Availability target is 99.9% for core endpoints.

[13:08] Miguel Torres: And if it’s down, do you fail open?

[13:10] Priya Natarajan: Console should degrade gracefully: show “Cost breakdown temporarily unavailable” and fall back to coarse aggregated numbers. Optimize will skip recommendation updates rather than serving bad advice.

[13:24] Hassan Mirza: Yeah, we would rather show “insufficient confidence / service unavailable” than push a change that increases cost.

---

[13:34] Samir Patel: Let’s talk about Dedicated vs Private. In Private, we might not want you calling home.

[13:41] Priya Natarajan: Totally. For Private, SCM can run inside your VPC/on-prem. Same service, different deployment topology. The spec is the same; you’d still provide model catalog metadata either by syncing or pinning versions.

[13:58] Samir Patel: Does that impact determinism?

[14:00] Jordan Lee: As long as you pin the same SCM version and model catalog snapshot, you’ll get deterministic outputs. We include version info in responses.

[14:10] Lena Wu: And quant profiles. Are those standardized?

[14:13] Aditya Rao: Yes, quant_profile_id is part of the input contract. We’ve seen confusion where people say “int8” but mean different calibration. We require a stable profile identifier.

[14:26] Lena Wu: We do some custom quant in house sometimes.

[14:29] Priya Natarajan: In Private, you can register your custom quant profile metadata. SCM needs at minimum expected compute delta and memory delta relative to baseline. If it’s unknown, again, we’ll tag as assumed and confidence drops.

---

[14:46] Grace Kim: How does this map to “showback per route”? We want per endpoint: /chat, /summarize, etc.

[14:55] Logan Wright: Route is a dimension we can carry, but we’re careful about cardinality. If you have 10,000 dynamic routes, we won’t tag them raw. The recommended approach is “route_group” or “policy_name.”

[15:10] Samir Patel: We can group. We have like 15 main features.

[15:13] Logan Wright: Perfect. Then Console can break down by route_group and model.

[15:19] Miguel Torres: And tenant? We’re multi-tenant.

[15:22] Priya Natarajan: Tenant/account is supported but access-controlled. That’s where audit logging comes in.

---

[15:32] Grace Kim: Audit logging… can you expand?

[15:35] Priya Natarajan: Any read of customer-level cost breakdown can be logged: who accessed, which tenant, what endpoint, and whether it included sensitive dimensions. We integrate with our existing audit pipeline.

[15:50] Samir Patel: Does that mean our users can see who internally at Redwood looked at cost data?

[15:54] Priya Natarajan: In Private you can. In Hosted/Dedicated, we have internal audit logs and can provide reports under enterprise support.

[16:04] Miguel Torres: Is cost breakdown considered sensitive?

[16:07] Priya Natarajan: We treat it as customer-sensitive because it can reveal usage patterns.

---

[16:16] Lena Wu: Going back to the breakdown: is “memory cost” real? Like you’re charging for VRAM?

[16:22] Aditya Rao: Not charging. It’s attribution. Some SKUs and some models become memory-bound; also KV cache can drive capacity. SCM can attribute that as an “opportunity cost” component or as overhead. In v1, we keep it simpler: compute dominates, memory is mostly expressed as overhead / capacity factor.

[16:44] Jordan Lee: We didn’t want v1 to pretend we can perfectly price VRAM. But we do want to highlight “you’re paying for long contexts” and “KV cache pressure.”

[16:56] Samir Patel: That’s fair.

---

[17:01] Hassan Mirza: From Optimize, the way it shows up is: if you have huge prompts, Optimize might recommend caching or prompt compression, and SCM can show the prefill cost drop. If you have lots of concurrent small requests, it might recommend increasing batch window slightly, and SCM can model batch efficiency vs latency.

[17:23] Miguel Torres: How do you incorporate latency constraints? Because batching can hurt p95.

[17:28] Hassan Mirza: Great question. Optimize couples SCM with latency models. SCM outputs cost; a separate model estimates latency under the candidate batch policy. We only recommend if cost improves and latency stays within SLO, or if you explicitly say “relax latency.”

[17:47] Samir Patel: So SCM itself doesn’t guarantee latency.

[17:50] Hassan Mirza: Correct, SCM is cost. But it can use telemetry like queue time to avoid over-crediting unrealistic batching.

---

[18:03] Logan Wright: One nuance: if we’re missing “queue_time_ms” or “batch_wait_ms” we can still estimate cost but we flag that we couldn’t validate the batching behavior.

[18:13] Lena Wu: So you need queue time too?

[18:16] Logan Wright: Optional but helpful. Required for certain explain modes; estimate mode can be done without.

[18:24] Grace Kim: Okay. So for our initial pilot, what is the minimum set we need to provide to get value?

[18:31] Aditya Rao: Minimum: model id, tokens in/out, region or gpu sku, and quant profile. If you can also provide cache hit rate, and effective batch, you’ll get much better breakdown.

[18:47] Samir Patel: For Hosted you already have those. For Private we’ll need to wire them.

---

[18:53] Priya Natarajan: Can I ask—are you evaluating Hosted, Dedicated, or Private? Just so we anchor the integration steps.

[19:00] Samir Patel: We’re likely Dedicated in the near term, maybe Private later. Data residency is a concern for one customer but not all.

[19:09] Grace Kim: Dedicated with some SLA is the expectation.

[19:13] Priya Natarajan: Okay, then telemetry is easiest. We already instrument the runtime. You’d consume SCM mainly via Console exports or via the API for internal pipelines.

[19:25] Miguel Torres: Are you okay with us calling SCM directly for our internal cost dashboards?

[19:30] Priya Natarajan: Yes, but we’ll scope rate limits and auth. It’s not a public endpoint yet; it’s more “enterprise/internal.” We can discuss.

---

[19:41] Lena Wu: Let’s do a concrete example. Suppose we have 2k input tokens and 200 output tokens on a llama-ish model. No cache. Batching is moderate. What would SCM likely say?

[19:54] Aditya Rao: Roughly you’d see prefill cost as the big chunk, decode smaller. If effective batch is, say, 4, you’d see a batch_savings line item relative to batch=1 baseline. If cache hit rate is 0, then cache_savings is 0.

[20:11] Jordan Lee: And if quant profile is int8, you’d see compute drop, but we’d also include an assumption about quality not being part of SCM. SCM doesn’t judge quality; Optimize uses evals separately.

[20:24] Samir Patel: Yeah quality is another can of worms.

---

[20:30] Grace Kim: Sorry, one more: how do you prevent people from interpreting SCM as “your bill will be this”?

[20:36] Aditya Rao: Great question. We label outputs as “estimated cost” and explicitly say “not used for billing.” Console copy will say “technical estimate for comparison.” And we include fields that show what assumptions were made.

[20:52] Priya Natarajan: Also we can include “billing_alignment: not_applicable” or something similar. Internally we’re strict: invoices come from metering/pricing services, not SCM.

---

[21:04] Samir Patel: What about reserved capacity? Dedicated pricing is like monthly. How do you translate to per-request cost?

[21:12] Aditya Rao: SCM can still attribute per-request consumption in normalized units. Then you can map your monthly commit to a blended rate if you want showback. We can provide a “rate table” that’s derived from your contract for internal accounting, but that’s optional.

[21:29] Grace Kim: That’s exactly what we want. Blended rate.

[21:33] Miguel Torres: But again, not invoice.

[21:35] Aditya Rao: Correct.

---

[21:41] Logan Wright: From telemetry standpoint, Dedicated makes it easier because we know the SKU and utilization. In Private, you have to tell us what rate you want to use.

[21:53] Lena Wu: Utilization… does SCM account for idle time?

[21:58] Aditya Rao: In v1, not fully. It’s mostly request-attributed cost. There is an optional “capacity_overhead_factor” if you want to allocate some idle. But we keep it explicit.

[22:12] Samir Patel: That’s fine. We can do separate idle allocation.

---

[22:18] Miguel Torres: I want to poke at failure modes. Suppose the SCM endpoint is slow. Does Console timeout?

[22:26] Priya Natarajan: Console clients should use short timeouts and fall back. We recommend 200ms budget for estimate in UI flows, with retries only on safe errors. For backend batch jobs you can do longer.

[22:42] Miguel Torres: Is it idempotent?

[22:44] Priya Natarajan: Yes. Requests can include an idempotency key. Estimate calls are pure functions; explain calls are read-only.

[22:55] Jordan Lee: And there’s version negotiation. Clients specify an “accept-version” header like scm.v1. If you request v2 and it’s not supported, you’ll get a structured error.

[23:08] Samir Patel: Good.

---

[23:11] Lena Wu: Can you talk about quant profile edge cases? We’ve seen int8 speedups vary by model.

[23:18] Aditya Rao: Yeah, that’s real. That’s why quant_profile metadata is keyed not just by “int8” but by “profile id” and model family compatibility.

[23:29] Jordan Lee: SCM will include an assumption if it’s using a generic delta. If we have measured deltas for that model family, it uses those. If not, it uses a default curve and flags lower confidence.

[23:43] Lena Wu: That’s acceptable.

---

[23:47] Samir Patel: Another thing: We sometimes do speculative decoding. Does SCM model that?

[23:53] Aditya Rao: Not in v1. We can represent it as a new cost component later. If speculative decoding changes decode compute, you’d see it through metered attribution if telemetry includes it, but the estimate path might not model it yet.

[24:10] Logan Wright: Telemetry can carry a flag like “decode_strategy=speculative,” but we’d need to standardize it. That’s future.

[24:18] Samir Patel: Understood.

---

[24:22] Grace Kim: I have a question on exports. Can we export cost breakdown per route per day?

[24:29] Priya Natarajan: Console will support per-route/model aggregation. For raw exports, we can provide an API that returns daily aggregates. Request-level explain is more for debugging.

[24:42] Grace Kim: That’s what we need.

---

[24:45] Hassan Mirza: And Optimize will effectively generate “recommended savings” by route_group. It will say like: “Enable caching for /answer endpoint; expected savings 18–25% given assumed hit rate.” That number comes from SCM scenario deltas.

[25:04] Samir Patel: Does Optimize keep track of whether the recommendation actually saved money?

[25:10] Hassan Mirza: Yes, we do pre/post analysis. We compare observed SCM attribution after change vs baseline. If confidence is low, we don’t claim savings.

[25:23] Logan Wright: That’s where metered attribution matters. We want to measure actual cache hit rates after enabling caching.

---

[25:31] Miguel Torres: Data retention—how long do you store the per-request signals used by explain?

[25:38] Logan Wright: Short retention by default, typically hours to a couple days depending on tier. Aggregates are longer. We can adjust for enterprise, but again, we avoid storing anything that looks like prompt content.

[25:54] Samir Patel: Okay.

---

[26:00] Lena Wu: What are the biggest ways customers get “wrong” cost numbers? Like where SCM could mislead.

[26:06] Aditya Rao: Three big ones:
1) Missing telemetry so we assume defaults (prefill/decode split, cache hit rate).
2) Mis-tagged quant profile or model version—people upgrade model and forget to update ids.
3) Cardinality trimming—if route grouping isn’t done, you might see “other” bucket and lose granularity.

[26:28] Jordan Lee: And one more: region/SKU missing. We had cases where region wasn’t set and validation failed, leading to $0 in some UIs. We now validate and return explicit errors.

[26:42] Grace Kim: $0 is exactly the kind of thing that causes panic.

[26:45] Priya Natarajan: Totally. That’s why we prefer “unavailable” over “0.”

---

[26:52] Samir Patel: On errors—what does the error model look like?

[26:56] Priya Natarajan: Structured error codes: invalid_input, unsupported_version, missing_required_signal, and internal. For missing signals, you can choose strict vs lenient. Strict fails; lenient returns with assumptions and lower confidence.

[27:16] Miguel Torres: That’s nice. We’d do strict in pipelines, lenient in UI.

[27:20] Priya Natarajan: Exactly.

---

[27:24] Grace Kim: Can you give us your recommended “minimum confidence” threshold?

[27:30] Hassan Mirza: For recommendations we use something like >=0.75 plus “no critical assumptions.” But we can tune. For showback dashboards you might accept lower if it’s directional.

[27:45] Samir Patel: We probably want 0.8 for anything automated.

[27:48] Aditya Rao: Makes sense.

---

[27:52] Lena Wu: Slight tangent: we also use OpenAI for some endpoints. Can SCM compare against that?

[27:59] Aditya Rao: SCM is about Redwood-served inference. But you can use our output schema and plug in external costs manually. Some customers build a blended dashboard.

[28:11] Grace Kim: We do that already.

[28:13] Samir Patel: We also tried Bedrock. Same story.

---

[28:18] Miguel Torres: If we move from Hosted to Dedicated later, do we lose historical comparisons?

[28:25] Priya Natarajan: Not if you keep the dimensions consistent. SCM version and model IDs remain. The only difference is the rate table changes. We can show “resource units” which are comparable across deployment modes.

[28:42] Jordan Lee: That’s a key design goal: cross-deployment comparability.

---

[28:47] Samir Patel: Great. I think the last big thing: what do you need from us right now to run a what-if?

[28:54] Hassan Mirza: Ideally: a sample workload profile per route_group: distribution of input/output tokens, concurrency, latency SLO, and any known cache patterns. Even a CSV is fine. Then we can run scenarios: batching window variations, caching on/off, quant profile changes, and show cost deltas with confidence.

[29:19] Lena Wu: We can provide that.

[29:21] Grace Kim: And we’d want assumptions clearly documented.

[29:25] Aditya Rao: Yes. We’ll include them.

---

[29:30] Priya Natarajan: Quick security note: if we enable explain in your environment, we’ll restrict who can call it. It can reveal per-tenant usage patterns. We’ll also audit log reads.

[29:44] Miguel Torres: That’s fine. We’ll probably gate it to SRE and platform.
